title: Reading (ch. 48)

lines: IN LENT, A BOOK FROM THE LIBRARY.
cards: When Lent begins, Saint Benedict's Rule says, each monk is handed a book from the library, and he's to read it straight through, from start to finish. Not skim it. Not sample a chapter and move on.

It's the same chapter as yesterday, chapter forty-eight, the one that called idleness the enemy. Yesterday was the work of the hands. But the chapter sets aside other hours, every day, for something just as deliberate.

teach.b: Benedict's timetable is careful. At certain hours the brothers work with their hands, and at certain hours they're free for holy reading.
The hours shift with the seasons, but the reading is always there, set into the day like the prayers.
This is what Catholics call lectio divina, holy reading, which you walked through step by step back around day two hundred thirty-three. It isn't reading for information, racing to the end.
It's slow: read scripture or a holy book, stop when a line catches, turn it over, let it sink, and maybe turn it into prayer.
The first psalm describes a person like that, in the Douay-Rheims: "on his law he shall meditate day and night." Benedict knows reading time can go soft.

teach.h: SENIORS CHECK NO ONE IS IDLE.
teach.b: So during the reading hours, one or two senior monks go around the monastery to make sure no brother is idle or chatting, bothering others instead of reading.
On Sunday, everyone is free for reading, except those with duties to do.

teach.h: IF HE CAN'T READ, HE'S GIVEN WORK.
teach.b: And if a brother is so careless that he can't or won't read, he's given some work, so he isn't idle. Even then, the answer is something useful, never nothing. What's striking is the respect the Rule gives to reading.

teach.h: ON HIS LAW HE SHALL MEDITATE DAY AND NIGHT.
teach.b: It isn't a hobby for the scholarly monks. It's a daily duty for everyone, at fixed hours, like prayer and work.
The hope behind it is that a few lines read slowly, day after day, can reshape a person, the way water shapes a stone.

how: Benedictine communities set aside time each day for lectio divina, the slow, prayerful reading of scripture, and some lay Catholics practice it on their own or in parish groups.

games.q: you're a senior monk walking the cloister during reading hours. a brother is chatting and distracting others. what are you there for?
o: to join the conversation and keep it friendly.
to make sure no one is idle or bothering others instead of reading.
to quiz each brother on what he's read.
games.why: Benedict sends one or two seniors around so the reading hours don't drift into idleness and chatter.

practice: Choose what you'd read slowly, a Gospel passage, a psalm, a page of a saint, or any book that feeds you, and when and where: a set hour, a chair, a corner, phone in another room.
Picture yourself reading one line, stopping, and reading it again, with no rush to the end of the page. If you pray, let the line you stop on become your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Reading. For Benedict, a daily duty at set hours: slow, holy reading, chewed rather than skimmed. Today's word.
